paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Otters are semi-aquatic, carnivorous mammals of the Mustelidae family, which includes skunks, weasels and badgers. With 13 different species, otters are quite diverse, but all display similar aquatic adaptations. They are sleek, streamlined swimmers with powerful jaws and sharp teeth. Most otters have webbing which extends for much of the length of each digit. An exception to this are the Asian short-clawed otters, which hunt for shrimps in ditches and paddy fields, and have no need of swimming speed. Otters' tails are stout at the base and taper towards the tip, where they flatten to form part of a propulsion unit. They have two layers of fur, consisting of an outer waterproof covering and a dense, fine, thermal layer underneath. The fur must be kept in good condition by grooming: salt water reduces its waterproofing and insulating qualities, which is why freshwater pools are important to coastal otters. To compensate for losing heat in water, otters have a metabolism rate which is 20 per cent higher than that of other, similarly sized mammals. Finally, otters' eyes and nostrils are placed high on the head so that they can see and breathe even when the rest of the body is submerged.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The otterine sense of smell is likely to be similar in sensitivity to that of dogs, but otters are probably short-sighted as their eyes are small. However, they do have the ability to modify the shape of the lens to make it more spherical, and hence overcome the refraction of light in water. In clear water and good light otters can hunt fish by sight, but even in murky water they can detect the presence of fish using the long whiskers that grow around the muzzle. These can sense the regular vibrations caused by the beat of a fish's tail as it swims away.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A number of constraints and preferences limit habitat selection. Otters are shy and wary creatures, and prefer territory where human activity does not impinge, and where no other otter groups are already in residence. A typical range for a male otter is 25 km. However, the productivity of the water affects this hugely, and one study found male ranges of between 12 and 80 km. Coastal otters in particular have a much more abundant food supply, and ranges for both males and females may be just a few kilometres of coastline. Throughout their home territory otters use a lot of different resting places, from holts beneath the roots of riverbank trees to flattened couches in dense vegetation such as reed beds.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Freshwater otters generally catch whichever fish are most readily available, particularly eels, while coastal otters commonly eat slow-moving, bottom-dwelling fish. However, the otter's diet varies, depending on the season. Frogs can become an important element during the breeding and hibernating seasons, and when eels burrow into the mud during winter, the more active fish like roach and trout become much easier to catch, as the cold water slows them down. Apart from fish, the most common prey are crayfish, crabs and water birds, which are grabbed from beneath. Small mammals such as moles are occasionally taken too.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Otters will breed at any time, depending on the availability of food. Gestation for Eurasian otters Is 63 days, and litter size varies from one to five, with two or three being the most common. Otter cubs first encounter the water at three months and hunt at eight months, but they are not fully independent until around nine months.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Otter species have been endangered for the past few decades. The plight of the British otter was recognised in the early 1960s, but it was not until the late 1970s that the chief cause was determined. Pesticides such as dieldrin and aldrin were first used in 1955 in agriculture and other industries, and are known to be very persistent. They had already been recognised as the cause of huge declines in the population of peregrine falcons, sparrow-hawks and other predators. These pesticides entered the river systems and the food chain-micro-organisms, fish and finally otters-with every step increasing their concentration. Although the chemicals began to be phased out from 1962, otter numbers continued to fall into the 1980s. This was probably due to habitat loss and road deaths, which, when acting upon populations which are already decimated, can make an entire population unviable, even if only a handful of individuals are lost.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In the few areas in Britain where otters remain, numbers are now beginning to recover. This is almost entirely due to conservation efforts, which have slowed or even reversed the destruction of suitable habitats, and the reintroduction of otters from captive breeding programmes. During the 1970s and '80s, water companies' cleaned up' many rivers by clearing trees from the banks, draining marshes and straightening water courses. Fortunately, these companies are now much more sensitive to environmental considerations and are in many cases actively reversing this trend. Voluntary conservation groups go even further, working to create otter havens, including stick piles and artificial dens made of drainpipes and bricks. Although some believe that reintroducing captive-bred otters should be a last resort as they are unlikely to survive, introducing individuals into a fragmented and fragile population may add just enough impetus for it to stabilise and expand rather than die out. Finally, the outlawing of otter hunting in 1978, coupled with the subsequent Wildlife and Countryside Act, has given otters full protection as an endangered species.
